verdicts.decisive_quote: Central estimate (0.25) falls within the 'yes' interval.
verdicts.verdict_one_line: An explicit abstention with zero cited evidence and a stated 50/50 split is silently converted into a 0.25 percent point estimate and a 0.65 'yes' call, after the reasoning itself says 'No boundary crossing is supported before the boundary audit' and ignores the one relevant datum in its own bank (May 2025 at 0.1 percent).

verdicts.decisive_quote: The net effect suggests inflation will be close to the target threshold, with potential to meet or exceed it.
verdicts.verdict_one_line: Its load-bearing upward drivers ('Inflationary pressures persist in core services, such as housing and transportation') are asserted content that its title-only 2023-2024 snippets do not contain and are labelled 'target_period_signal' despite being one to two years stale, while the only quantity it actually has (May at 0.1 percent, which it concedes is 'below the target threshold') points the other way, so the 0.65 'yes' reads as assembled around a pre-chosen option.

verdicts.decisive_quote: A report indicated that core inflation in May rose to 2.7%, which is significantly above the target threshold and contradicts the 0.1% figure.
verdicts.verdict_one_line: Direction, estimate (0.12 percent) and option mapping cohere and counterevidence is surfaced rather than buried, but it manufactures a false conflict by comparing a year-over-year core PCE rate to a month-over-month CPI threshold, and its 'surging electricity prices' driver sits in the energy component that core CPI excludes.

verdicts.decisive_quote: it does not explicitly state 'core CPI' and is for the preceding month, making its direct applicability to the target metric and period partial
verdicts.verdict_one_line: The cleanest grounding of the seven: it uses the single relevant datum without overstating it, names the headline-versus-core mismatch as an unverified step, and derives 'no' unambiguously from a 0.1 percent estimate against a 0.185 threshold; weakened by a bare persistence mechanism with no named price drivers and an unexplained hardening from 0.75 in the reasoning to 0.85 in the forecast.

verdicts.decisive_quote: The evidence for May 2025 indicates a monthly inflation change of 0.1%, which is below the 0.185% threshold. This strongly suggests the target will not be met.
verdicts.verdict_one_line: Reaches 'no' coherently but overreaches: it grades magnitude support as 'supported' while its own evidence_fit says the metric match is only partial, relabels a headline CPI print as 'monthly core CPI change', leans on absence of evidence as counterevidence, and puts 0.85-0.90 on 'no' even though its own stated range of 0.05 to 0.25 percent straddles the 0.185 threshold.

verdicts.decisive_quote: Moderate uncertainty exists because the forecast relies on extrapolating the trend from May 2025 to June 2025, and past data shows inflation can deviate from expectations. The exact drivers of core CPI for June 2025 are not fully detailed in the provided evidence.
verdicts.verdict_one_line: The only trace whose interval does work: a 0.07 to 0.19 percent range with a top edge just above the threshold coherently justifies leaving 0.15 on 'yes', and the upside counterevidence is raised and resolved rather than dropped; marked down for treating mid-2023 and late-2023 headline-only snippets as current disinflation drivers and for grading magnitude support 'supported' while its own metric match is 'partial'.

verdicts.decisive_quote: Magnitude support for the 0.185% threshold is absent.
verdicts.verdict_one_line: Best-calibrated of the set, holding mass at 0.60/0.40 to match a declared directional conflict and absent magnitude support, but it inherits historical DAG labels onto current sources (a core PCE 'Fed's preferred gauge' item is renamed 'May 2025 Core CPI Level', an ECB services piece becomes 'Services PPI inflation'), and having declared direction 'uncertain' it anchors the central estimate at 0.1 percent without saying why, so 'no' is consistent but not entailed.

ranking_rationale: The top traces anchored on the one quantity either bank actually contained, stated plainly what that quantity could not tell them about core CPI in June, and let the option mapping and the probability mass follow from that admitted limit. The bottom two either asserted driver content their title-only snippets never carried or, in direct_forecast's case, declared an explicit abstention and then produced a 0.25 percent point estimate and a 0.65 'yes' out of it.
shared_evidence_note: Both banks carried the same decisive item (CNBC, US inflation up 0.1 percent in May), and E1's extra core PCE and tariff/electricity items only widened stated uncertainty rather than flipping direction, so the yes/no split is a reasoning difference, not an evidence difference: direct_forecast and structured_reasoning read the same E0 as the three E0 methods that concluded 'no'.
